text: Hospital fasting orders and swallowing difficulties can cause missed medication; the pharmacy review recommends planning alternative administration and obtaining specialist or pharmacist input for enteral conversion when needed. (low confidence)

text: A pharmacy-informatics review proposes that, when adding a medicine to the hospital formulary is not feasible, the inpatient pharmacy identify patient-owned supplies and have them re-labeled for use during the stay, and it notes that the FDA Orange Book defines therapeutic equivalency; the Parkinson's Foundation safe and contraindicated medications document states that medications, even in the same class, are usually not interchangeable and that patients should be allowed to supply their own medications if not on formulary. (medium confidence)
keywords: PD medication timing, interactions and hospital safety

text: The pharmacy review reports that high-protein meals can reduce levodopa absorption and suggests coordinating meal delivery with medication times when feasible. (low confidence)

text: NICE NG71 states that people with Parkinson's disease who are admitted to hospital or care homes should have their medicines given at the appropriate times, which in some cases may mean allowing self-medication, and adjusted by, or only after discussion with, a specialist in the management of Parkinson's disease; a pharmacy-informatics review describes electronic order entry that can mistranscribe a patient's specific medication times and intervals. (medium confidence)
keywords: PD medication timing, interactions and hospital safety

text: NICE advises against abrupt withdrawal or sudden failure of antiparkinsonian treatment from poor absorption because of the risk of acute akinesia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome; drug holidays should not be used. (low confidence)

text: A pharmacy-informatics review states that medications affecting dopaminergic states must be used cautiously in Parkinson's disease, and singles out dopamine antagonists in the antipsychotic class (including haloperidol) and the antiemetic class (including metoclopramide, promethazine and prochlorperazine) as able to worsen Parkinson motor function. (medium confidence)
keywords: PD medication timing, interactions and hospital safety

text: NICE advises that hospital or care-home medication changes should be made by, or discussed with, a Parkinson specialist, and that appropriate dose timing may sometimes require self-medication. (low confidence)

text: A pharmacy workflow review recommends treating levodopa as time-critical, documenting administration times and reasons for deviations, and using overdue alerts and custom order times. Its proposed 30-minute window is an operational recommendation, not proof that every patient can safely tolerate that delay. (low confidence)
keywords: PD medication timing, interactions and hospital safety

text: A pharmacy-informatics review states that pharmacist medication reconciliation involves checking dose, route, frequency and timing against the home regimen, with confirmation from the patient, care partner or outpatient records. (low confidence)
keywords: PD medication timing, interactions and hospital safety

text: The Parkinson Foundation advises updating a written medication form whenever the routine changes and keeping a supply of current medicines in labeled pharmacy bottles for hospital use. (low confidence)
keywords: PD medication timing, interactions and hospital safety

text: NICE limits its discussion of protein redistribution to people taking levodopa who experience motor fluctuations, and specifically advises against reducing total daily protein intake. (low confidence)
keywords: PD medication timing, interactions and hospital safety

text: The APOKYN label contraindicates concomitant use of apomorphine with ondansetron, listed among serotonin receptor antagonists, following reports of profound hypotension and loss of consciousness. (low confidence)

text: The Foundation hospital checklist warns about mixing MAO-B inhibitors with listed pain medicines and calls for consultation among the Parkinson clinician, surgeon and anesthesiologist; this checklist does not establish identical interaction risks for every listed agent. (low confidence)

text: The Foundation cautions that benzodiazepines and other medicines for sleep or pain can contribute to confusion, hallucinations and falls; its acute-agitation advice limits repeated benzodiazepine use to avoid worsening confusion. (low confidence)
